# Pushguard

> Org-wide push monitoring for GitHub. One GitHub App install watches every repository in your organization, evaluates each push against your detection rules, and files a GitHub issue naming the pushing account when something looks wrong: force pushes, new install hooks, workflow tampering, committed secrets, or obfuscated payloads.

Built for the attack where a compromised teammate account force-pushes code that
executes on everyone else's machine at the next `git pull && npm install`.

Two ways in. Watching is the product; scanning is how you see what it finds
before you install anything.

- **Watch**: push -> webhook -> rule engine -> diff fetch only if a rule needs
  one -> optional AI review -> issue in the repository that was pushed. A push
  that matches nothing costs zero GitHub API calls.
- **Scan**: reads the last 50 commits already committed to a branch, stores
  findings, files nothing on GitHub until you say so.

Key properties, because they are the questions people actually ask:

- Rules belong to your account, not one organization. One rule set is evaluated
  against every org you installed on; narrow a rule with its `repos` globs.
- Alerts are GitHub issues, filed in the repository that triggered them, public
  or private. A public repository gets the alert but not the evidence: matched
  lines are withheld so an alert about a committed secret does not become an
  indexed copy of it. High and critical alerts @mention your alert contact.
- Authorization is GitHub's answer, not ours. A scan is authorized against the
  requesting user's own GitHub token, never the installation token, which sees
  more than any single member is entitled to.
- Force pushes are read from the orphaned side. A rewrite makes the old tip
  unreachable, so a checkout, and every scanner reading one, sees only the
  survivors. Pushguard compares in both directions and runs content rules
  against the difference, reporting what a force push *erased* rather than only
  that it happened. A secret committed and then force-pushed away is still
  leaked, and this is what reports it.
- Path rules cost zero GitHub API calls; the webhook payload already lists
  changed files. Content rules fetch one compare diff with a 2 MB read budget,
  and lines are matched in full with no length cap. Exceeding the budget files a
  finding of its own rather than a footnote: an unread diff is a blind spot, and
  the answer is "we did not look", not "nothing found".
- AI review is advisory and escalate-only. A rule match files a ticket
  regardless of what the AI says.
- AI rules are their own kind of rule, not a field on a pattern rule. They fire
  on their own `paths`, so they can find what no pattern was written for.
  `scope: changed` reads the files a push touched; `scope: repository` runs as a
  background session where the model navigates the tree through two tools,
  `read_file` and `find_references`, with every path validated against the
  rule's own scope. The model never holds a credential: it names a path and the
  server decides whether it gets one.
- `find_references` answers from a code index built at install and maintained by
  the push webhook. It stores paths and identifiers, never source, and costs no
  GitHub call at review time.
- A model that could not answer is reported, never treated as a clean result.
  Timeouts, rate limits, truncation and partial indexes each file a finding, for
  the same reason an unread diff does: a reader cannot tell "we did not look"
  from "nothing found".
- No cache and no TTL anywhere. Stored GitHub data is a projection maintained by
  webhooks, not a copy with a guess about when it went stale.
- Limits: 25 scans a day, 20 repositories each, one at a time per account.
- Multi-tenant. One deployment serves any number of organizations.
- Self-hostable, MIT licensed, Next.js and MongoDB.

## Product

- [Home](/): what Pushguard detects and why force-push attacks matter.
- [How to use](/how-to-use): five steps from install to first alert.
- [Dashboard](/dashboard): alert feed, scans, and rule editing. Requires GitHub sign-in.

## Rules

A rule is YAML. All conditions on it must hold; each rule is evaluated
independently.

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `repos`, `branches` | glob scoping, empty means all; `acme/*` binds a rule to one org |
| `paths`, `exclude_paths`, `change_type` | changed-file conditions |
| `all_of` | groups of globs, each of which must be matched by a file in the same push |
| `when` | push conditions: `forced`, `sender_first_push`, `branch_created`, `branch_deleted`, `hour_utc`, `author_mismatch`, `unreviewed` |
| `added_lines` | regex against added diff lines, case-sensitive, no flags |
| `commit_message` | regex against each commit's subject line |
| `unicode_risk` | `controls` for Trojan Source (bidi overrides, invisible characters), `confusables` adds homoglyphs; language-independent |
| (AI rules are separate) | a rule carrying a `prompt` instead of a pattern |
| `severity` | `low`, `medium`, `high`, `critical`; high and above mention your alert contact |

A scan cannot answer every rule. Rules keyed on the push event (`when`) and
Push-event rules are dropped before a scan evaluates, because a snapshot of
committed code has nothing to answer them with. That is the honest limit of
scanning, and the reason to install.

- [Rule schema by example](https://github.com/saadiqayyum/Ironman/blob/main/public/rules.example.yaml)
- [Rule catalog](https://github.com/saadiqayyum/Ironman/tree/main/lib/rules/catalog): 78 rules in 16 packs, shipped as code rather than seeded per account. Ecosystem packs self-scope by `paths`, so nobody declares what language a repository is.
- [Rule engine](https://github.com/saadiqayyum/Ironman/blob/main/lib/engine.ts): glob matching via picomatch, content matching via RegExp.

## API

Session-authenticated JSON, same origin as the dashboard. There is no API token
and no public endpoint.

- `GET /api/scan-targets`: installations and repositories you may scan.
- `GET /api/scan-branches`: branches of one repository you may scan.
- `POST /api/scans`: queue a scan of one repository or a whole account.
- `GET /api/scans/{id}`: scan status and findings.
- `POST /api/scans/{id}/file`: file a finished scan's findings as GitHub issues.
- `GET /api/alerts`, `POST /api/alerts/bulk`: alert feed and bulk acknowledge.
- `GET|POST /api/rules`, `PATCH /api/rules/{id}`, `POST /api/rules/test`,
  `POST /api/rules/import`, `GET /api/rules/export`.
- `POST /api/webhook`: GitHub App webhook receiver, signature-verified.
- `GET /api/health`.

## Setup

- [README](https://github.com/saadiqayyum/Ironman/blob/main/README.md): full operator setup, GitHub App permissions, webhook events, and the Vercel deploy.

Required GitHub App permissions: Metadata read, Contents read, Issues read and
write, Organization Members read. Pushguard deliberately does not request
`administration`, so it cannot create repositories.

Pushguard is a detection layer. Turn on prevention too: an org ruleset blocking
force pushes on default branches, mandatory 2FA, and
`npm config set ignore-scripts true` on developer machines.
